rules.rule: Values of different types are never equal, even when one would convert to the other or both hold the same elements
Tuples holding nulls of different types are unequal, because their tuple types differ
Two nulls compared directly are equal whatever their types, including a null string and the null keyword (disputed)

Two strings are equal when their NFC normalizations are identical: composition, canonical reordering of combining marks, singleton mappings and Hangul composition all apply, including inside tuples and attribute names
String equality applies no normalization beyond NFC, so compatibility equivalents and a letter with and without a combining accent are unequal
Two bools are equal exactly when both are true or both are false
Two tuples of identical type are equal exactly when every pair of corresponding elements is equal by the rules of the element type, recursively
Two objects of identical type are equal exactly when every attribute is equal, whatever order the attributes were written in

Structural types are identical only if they are of the same kind with the same attribute names or element count and identical attribute or element types, so values of other structural types are unequal
Two lists of identical type are equal exactly when they have the same length and equal elements in the same order
Two sets of identical type are equal exactly when each holds every element of the other, in any order
Two maps of identical type are equal exactly when they have the same keys with equal values
Collection types are identical only if they are of the same kind with identical element types, so collections of different kinds or element types are unequal, even when empty
A capsule type is identical only to itself, and the calling application defines equality of its values
rules.untested: The protocol has no encoding for capsule values, and implementations need not support capsule types

rules.rule: No operations other than application-defined equality and application functions apply to capsule values
rules.untested: The protocol has no encoding for capsule values, and implementations need not support capsule types

rules.rule: A type matches a type specification that is identical to it, for tuple, object, list, set and map types

Any type matches the dynamic pseudo-type, also nested as an element, attribute or collection element type, while the rest of the type must still match: a list of strings or of maps matches a list of the dynamic pseudo-type, and an object doesn't
A set of strings passed for a list of the dynamic pseudo-type, which the spec's own example says doesn't match, is converted to a list of strings (disputed)

A type that isn't identical to a type specification and doesn't match it through the dynamic pseudo-type doesn't match, such as a tuple of another length or with an element of another type, a list, set or map of another element type, an object with an attribute of another type, or a tuple of elements with no common type for a list of the dynamic pseudo-type
The null keyword or an empty tuple passed for a list of the dynamic pseudo-type becomes a null or empty list with the dynamic pseudo-type as its element type (disputed)

A list, set or map holding an empty collection and a non-empty one, both collections of collections, is an error for its own type with the dynamic pseudo-type as the innermost element type, because the empty collection converts to a collection whose element type holds the dynamic pseudo-type while the non-empty one keeps its own element type (disputed)
A null value is equal to a null of the same type
A null value is not equal to any non-null value, including zero and the empty string
A conditional whose predicate is null, whether the null keyword or a typed null, is an error (disputed)

An arithmetic, comparison or logic operator with a null operand is an error, except that hashicorp/hcl's short circuits make null || true true, and null && true false because they treat the null as not true (disputed)
Interpolating a null, whether the null keyword or a typed null, into a template with other parts is an error (disputed)
Indexing into a null collection is an error, even if its type can be indexed, and so is indexing with a null key
Accessing an attribute of a null object is an error, even if the object type has that attribute
Calling applications should treat an attribute whose value is null as if it were absent
rules.untested: This is guidance for calling applications about attribute values; schema processing only looks for a definition, so a required attribute whose value is null is present (native/structure/schema-required-attribute-null)

rules.rule: A function call passing null to a parameter that doesn't accept null is an error, whether the null is the null keyword or typed, a variadic argument or an expanded element, and even when an earlier argument is unknown or a later one is the dynamic value
A positional or variadic parameter that accepts null receives a null argument, the null keyword or a typed null, and an argument that only holds a null is not a null argument
Converting a value to its own type leaves it unchanged
An unsafe conversion is an error for a source value that has no corresponding value in the target type
A null converts to a null of the target type, keeping the target type
A null converts to another type only if its own type converts to it, so a null number used as a || operand and a null bool for a number parameter that accepts null are errors (disputed)
An empty list, set or map converted to the same kind of collection of the dynamic pseudo-type keeps its element type, as it would if it had elements
true converts to the string true and false to the string false
The strings true and 1 convert to true, and the strings false and 0 convert to false
Any other string fails to convert to bool, including other capitalizations, added spaces, the empty string, other words and other spellings of one
A number converts to the decimal digits of its integer part, then a period and the fractional digits only if the fractional part isn't zero, with a minus sign for negative numbers
Negative zero converts to the string -0 (disputed)
Positive infinity converts to the string +Inf and negative infinity to -Inf (disputed)
Number to string conversion never uses an exponent, however large or small the number
Number to string conversion writes the number at full precision, including integers beyond 64 bits and binary fractions beyond float64 precision
A string of decimal digits, optionally with a minus sign and a fractional part, converts to the number it spells, at full precision
A string that isn't in the number syntax fails to convert to number: surrounding spaces, hexadecimal, underscores, NaN, non-ASCII digits and the empty string
A string with a decimal exponent (e) or a binary exponent (p) converts to the number it spells (disputed)
A string with a leading plus sign, a leading or trailing period, or the spelling inf converts to a number (disputed)
There is no conversion in either direction between bool and number: not for operands, predicates or index keys
A set converts to a list holding the same elements
Set elements become list elements in an order the spec leaves undefined
rules.untested: The order is implementation-defined, and a portable test can't depend on it

rules.rule: Converting the same set to a list more than once gives its elements in the same order each time

A set holding an unknown element and another element converts to an unknown list, because the unknown element may equal the other one, so the list's length isn't known, and a map of such sets converts to a map of lists
A set holding an unknown element converted to a list of another element type gives an unknown list of the set's own element type (disputed)
Converting a tuple with equal elements to a set keeps one of them, as hashicorp/hcl does when a set and a tuple unify to a set (disputed)
A tuple converts to a list when every element converts to the list's element type, converting each element
A tuple converts to a set when every element converts to the set's element type, converting each element, including the elements after one that already has that type

A tuple doesn't convert to a set when one of its elements doesn't convert to the set's element type, whether the element's type has no such conversion, even in an unknown tuple, or its value fails to convert
An object converts to a map when every attribute converts to the map's element type, with attribute names as keys

hashicorp/hcl has no conversion from a list or set to a tuple, so a list argument for a tuple parameter of the same length is an error, and a list and a tuple of another length unify to a list instead of failing the spec's length check (disputed)

When a map and an object that converts to the map's type unify, hashicorp/hcl keeps the map, so the map keeps its keys even when they don't match the object's attributes; it converts a map argument for an object parameter, but drops map keys that aren't attributes of the object type instead of failing (disputed)
A map without an element for one of an object type's attributes doesn't convert to that object type
Converting a map value to an object type drops every map key that isn't an attribute of the object type, also one that sorts before the attributes, instead of failing (disputed)
An object converts to an object type with the same attribute names by converting each attribute value

hashicorp/hcl never converts an object to an object type with attributes it lacks, which the spec fills with null: objects with different attribute names unify to a map, and such an object argument for an object parameter is an error (disputed)
Converting an object to an object type that lacks some of its attributes drops them and keeps the attributes the type has, including ones that sort after a dropped one
Converting an object to an object type fails when an attribute's value has no conversion to that attribute's type in the target
A tuple converts to another tuple type of the same length when each element converts
Converting a set of strings to a list of numbers is unsafe and fails for a string that isn't a number, which hashicorp/hcl attempts when a list of numbers and a set of strings unify (disputed)

Converting a map of sets to a map of lists, where one set holds an unknown element, turns that set into an unknown list of the set's own element type and then unifies the map's elements with safe conversions only, which fails where only unsafe conversions exist and, for element types holding the dynamic pseudo-type, can give maps or lists of it in place of the objects or tuples asked for (disputed)

Converting an unknown value whose type converts to the target type gives an unknown value of the target type: an unknown map to another map type or to an object type, also one with an optional attribute that the map's elements can't convert to, and an unknown list to a set type

Converting an unknown value to a type containing the dynamic pseudo-type gives an unknown whose type has the value's own types in place of the dynamic pseudo-type: an unknown map's element type, an unknown object's attribute type, and for an unknown object converted to a map or an unknown tuple converted to a list, the unification of its attribute or element types, where a dynamic attribute or element gives way to a string one

Converting an unknown list to a set of any gives an unknown set of the list's element type, and converting an unknown tuple to a set of any gives an unknown set of the unification of the tuple's element types

A converted unknown that came from one that may be null may be null too, and an unknown list converted to a set may have fewer elements than the list, since equal elements merge, so comparing the converted unknown with null or with a shorter set gives an unknown bool
An unknown list that may be empty converts to a set that may be empty too, so comparing the converted unknown with an empty set gives an unknown bool

A converted unknown keeps what hashicorp/hcl knows about the unknown it came from: one that can't be null still can't be, and an unknown list converted to another list type keeps its range of lengths, so comparing it with null or with a list whose length is outside that range gives false (disputed)

An unknown list known to hold at least one element converts to a set known to hold at least one too, since merging equal elements can't empty a set, so comparing the converted unknown with an empty set gives false (disputed)
An empty tuple converts to a set of any, and an empty object to a map of any, giving an empty collection although there are no element types to unify
Converting an object to a map whose element type is a collection type containing any unifies the types of the converted attributes, so a list of numbers and a list of strings become lists of strings
Converting to a list, set or map whose element type is a collection type containing any is an error when the converted elements have no common type, also beside a list holding only null

Converting a tuple to a set whose element type is a collection type containing any, or an object to a map whose element type is a tuple type containing any, doesn't unify the converted elements, so a list or tuple of a number and one of a string are an error, unlike in a list (disputed)
Converting to a collection of any is an error when the element types have no common type, even if one more element is the null keyword or of the dynamic pseudo-type, also for an unknown tuple
A tuple whose elements are all the null keyword converts to a list of any holding those nulls, and to a set of any holding a single null, since equal elements merge (disputed)

An unknown object whose attribute types have no common type, one of them the dynamic pseudo-type, converts to an unknown map of any instead of failing as such a tuple does for a list of any (disputed)
When two types convert to each other, unification picks the one reached by a safe conversion, so number or bool with string gives string, in either branch
Bool and number fail to unify, also as collection element types, although both convert to string (disputed)
Two collection types of the same kind unify to that kind of collection of their unified element types, or fail if the element types don't unify
A list type and a set type with unifiable element types unify to a list type
A list of numbers and a set of strings unify to a list of numbers, because the set's strings convert to numbers unsafely (disputed)
A map type and an object type that converts to it unify to the map type, converting the object (disputed)
A list type and a tuple type unify to a list type, and a set type and a tuple type unify to a set type (disputed)

A list of numbers unified with a tuple of strings, or a map of numbers unified with an object of strings, converts the numbers in the places of the tuple's or object's strings to strings, also when the tuple holds the null keyword beside its strings

A list of maps and a tuple of objects with differing attribute types, unified to the list type, fail when the tuple is the chosen result, because hashicorp/hcl converts the original tuple instead of its converted elements (disputed)

A tuple unified with a list type, or an object unified with a map type, fails when it is the selected result and its elements don't convert to the type they unify to among themselves, even when they convert to the unified list or map type (disputed)
A tuple of numbers unified with a list of strings, or an object of numbers unified with a map of strings, converts to that list or map type, so its numbers become strings (disputed)
The dynamic pseudo-type unifies with another type to that type, both for a whole result and for a tuple element of primitive type
A collection whose element type is the dynamic pseudo-type and a collection of the same kind with a primitive element type unify to the second collection's type, converting the first (disputed)
A dynamic tuple element unified with an object element keeps the dynamic pseudo-type instead of taking the object type (disputed)
A tuple nested in the selected result of a conditional is returned unchanged when the other result has the null keyword in its place
A dynamic tuple element unified with a map, list, set or tuple element keeps the dynamic pseudo-type instead of taking the other element's type (disputed)
Unifying only dynamic pseudo-types gives the dynamic pseudo-type
Types with no common type, such as an object type and string, unify to the dynamic pseudo-type when it is one of them (disputed)
Two object types with the same attribute names unify attribute by attribute to an object type, or fail if some attribute types don't unify
Two object types with different attribute names unify to a map of their unified attribute types, or fail if those types don't unify (disputed)

When objects with different attribute names unify, an attribute read from the result keeps its own type and the selected value if the other attributes are the null keyword, an empty object or tuple, or a map or list of the dynamic pseudo-type
Two tuple types of the same length unify element by element to a tuple type, or fail if some element types don't unify

Objects with the same attribute names, or tuples of the same length, fail to unify when the types of one attribute or element don't unify, even when all their attribute or element types would unify as the element type of a map or list (disputed)
Tuple types of different lengths unify to a list of their unified element types (disputed)
Tuple types of different lengths fail to unify when their elements have no common type, also when some of those elements are tuples of different lengths
Unification can produce a type that is none of its input types
Unification fails if one of the types can't convert to the type the rules select
Types whose kinds have no unification rule, such as tuple and object, list and map, or a primitive and a structural type, fail to unify
Unification rules combine: a set of numbers and a list of strings unify to a list of strings
Among three or more types, the dynamic pseudo-type takes the type the others unify to, whether it comes before or after them (disputed)

A map type and an object type that can't convert to it unify to the object type, converting the map, as for a map of the dynamic pseudo-type and an object whose attribute types don't unify, also beside a second map of the same type
Three or more list and set types unify to a list of the type their elements unify to: tuples element by element, and collections by their own element types at every level

Among three or more types, objects with the same attribute names unify attribute by attribute, and when objects have different attributes or swap the types of their attributes, a string in the first object stays a string in the result
Where three or more types hold a list, a set and a tuple type in the same place, those unify to the list or the tuple type, never the set type (disputed)
A collection of tuples with dynamic pseudo-type elements unifies with collections of tuples whose elements in those places don't unify, such as a set of strings and a set of lists (disputed)
List, set and map values have no native syntax, but values from variables keep their collection types, including nested ones
The null keyword is a null of the dynamic pseudo-type
